paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.68(2):1 Rule 3.68(2)—Non-disclosure of action or defence See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2). 1. What Is a Cause of Action? A cause of action is a set of facts which, if established, would entitle the plaintiff to some form of relief. Scotia Mortgage Corp. v. Goss (1987), 83 A.R. 15 at 18 (Master). 2. Test In Rudichuk v. Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 132, 2019 CarswellAlta 336, Madam Justice Marriott gave this summary of the law as it relates to applications to strike a claim on the basis that it does not disclose a reasonable claim: [8] Rule 3.68(1)(a) and (2)(b) provide that all or part of a claim may be struck out where it “discloses no reasonable claim”. As established by the Supreme Court of Canada, it is accepted that a court should only strike a claim if it is plain and obvious that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action: Hunt v T&N plc, 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC), [1990] 2 SCR 959 and Knight v Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd, 2011 SCC 42 (CanLII). It is only if a claim has no reasonable prospect of success, then it should be struck, and so long as the plaintiff has some chance of success and the claim is arguable, then the Court should allow the matter to proceed to trial: Hunt at 989; Imperial Tobacco at para 17. [9] Further, the Supreme Court of Canada has held that it is not determinative that the law has not yet recognized a particular claim and a court should be generous and err on the side of permitting a novel, but arguable claim to proceed to trial: Imperial Tobacco at para 21. Thus, the statement of claim should be struck “only if it is clear that in law the case cannot succeed, based on principles directly applicable to the case as set out in the pleadings”: Anger v Berkshire Investment Group Inc, 2001 CanLII 24141 (ON CA), [2001] OJ No 379 (CA) at para 15. [10] When applying this test, the Court may examine a number of factors, including the clarity of the factual pleadings and the existence of case law discussing similar causes of action: NEP Canada ULC v MEC OP LLC, 2014 ABCA 140 (CanLII) at para 16. However, the parties may not submit new evidence on this application: Rules, r 3.68(3). In considering the claim, the court must assume that the facts as pleaded are true: Hunt at 980. Finally, the defendant bears the burden of proof on this application, and the onus to meet is “extremely high”: Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre v CBC, 2012 ABQB 48 (CanLII) at para 29. … [13] On an application to strike a claim when the issue in question is duty of care, the court need not determine “whether a duty of care will be recognized, but whether it is plain and obvious that no duty of care can be recognized”: Haskett v Equifax Canada Inc (2003), 2003 CanLII 32896 (ON CA), 63 OR (3d) 577 (CA) at para 24. In Alexander v. Pacific Trans-Ocean Resources Ltd. (1991), 115 A.R. 317 (Q.B.), at 318-19, [; affirmed (1992) 120 A.R. 22 (C.A.)], Justice Perras said: As well, I keep in mind the admonition of Wilson, J., in Hunt v. T & N plc et al. (1990), 117 N.R. 321 (S.C.C.), when she said at pp. 345-346: Thus, the test in Canada governing the application of provisions like rule 19(24)(a) of the British Columbia Rules of Court is the same as the one that governs an application under R.S.C., Order 18, r. 19: assuming that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it ‘plain and obvious’ that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be ‘driven from the judgment seat’. Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the others listed in rule 19(24) of the British Columbia Rules of Court should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out under rule 19(24)(a). It is noted that r. 19(24)(a) of the British Columbia Supreme Court is for all intents and purposes the same as r. 129(1)(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court. The same test was adapted by Wachowich J. in Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Prisco (1990), 115 A.R. 184 at 187-88 (Q.B.). In Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, Wilson J., speaking for the court, said at p. 344: Indeed, I would go so far as to suggest that where a statement of claim reveals a difficult and important point of law, it may well be critical that the action be allowed to proceed. Only in this way can we be sure that the common law in general, and the law of torts in particular, will continue to evolve to meet the legal challenges that arise in our modern industrial society. In Hirtz v. Alberta (Public Trustee) (1997), 221 A.R. 324 (Q.B.), at pp. 335-36, Moreau J. specifically quoted the above-noted passage from Wilson J.'s judgment in Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959. And Fruman J. has provided the following summary of the applicable principles: The principles which apply in respect of a motion to strike out pleadings have been stated in many cases and do not seem to be at issue in these proceedings. In Hunt v. T & N plc, (sub nom. Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.) [1990] 6 W.W.R. 385 (S.C.C.), Wilson J. summarized the relevant principles. At p. 400, she stated that the Supreme Court of Canada has consistently upheld the “plain and obvious” test. At p. 401, she phrased the question as follows: “… assuming that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it ‘plain and obvious’ that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action?” She confirms that: Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect … should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be struck … Wilson J. confirms that an application to strike pleadings is not an appropriate forum in which to engage in a detailed examination of the strengths and weaknesses of the plaintiff's case. One is to assume that all facts alleged by the plaintiff are true, and then determine whether the plaintiff can present a question “fit to be tried”. Wilson J. considered other Supreme Court of Canada decisions and indicated that following these decisions “the test remained whether the outcome of the case was ‘plain and obvious’ or ‘beyond reasonable doubt’”. I believe that this summary of the principles is also an enumeration of the principles used in Alberta in connection with a motion to strike under R. 129 …Rocky Mountain Rail Society v. H & D Hobby Distributing Ltd. (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 424 at 427-28 (Q.B.). Madam Justice Fruman then drew a distinction between “novel legal propositions” (which normally are not to be struck) and “broadening a narrowly defined tort” (which might be struck). At p. 431 of Rocky Mountain Rail Society, her Ladyship said: While judges should not be quick to strike pleadings which raise novel legal propositions, I do not see this matter as a novel proposition but rather as a broadening of a narrowly defined tort. No public policy reasons have been suggested to justify such an extension, which would open the floodgates of this type of pleading and would put Rocky Mountain and its directors to the time and expense of defending an action that is doomed to failure. In Manulife Financial Services Ltd. v. BTK Holdings Ltd. (1997), 56 Alta. L.R. (3d) 355 (Master), Master Funduk noted that “novel” does not encompass “far-fetched”. At p. 360, the learned Master said: It also does not help to say that a pleading should not be struck out where it raises something novel. Novel does not encompass something that is plain and obvious beyond doubt. The answer to that (said in another context) is: It is true that in one decision I said the test is what is arguable. It must be understood, of course, that that means reasonably arguable. In a sense almost any proposition (except maybe whether two plus two equals four) is arguable. But it cannot be a far-fetched argument; it cannot be an argument that is contrary to binding authority. (Mocyk v. Municipal District of East Peace No. 131 (Oct. 10, 1995), C.A. 9503-0257-A.C., Côté J.A.) Novel does not encompass far-fetched. The Court of Appeal in Korte v. Deloitte, Haskins & Sells (1993), 8 Alta. L.R. (3d) 337, 1993 CarswellAlta 304, 135 A.R. 389 (C.A.), noted that specific words need not be pleaded to set forth a cause of action—the test is whether the essence of the cause of action is set forth in the pleading. At p. 340, the court said: The court should also allow for some generosity in assessing whether the statement of claim discloses a cause of action, and it is not always necessary to plead specific words or specific legal conclusions providing that the essence of the action is outlined in the pleadings. In Tanar Industries Ltd. v. American Home Assurance Co. (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 144 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal noted that if a chambers judge dismisses an application under R. 129(1)(a), an appeal ought to be allowed only if it is obvious that there is no cause of action. At p. 147, the court, per curiam, said: In addition, this Court must have regard to the standard of review that is relevant in appeals of this sort. Appellate courts will not lightly interfere with discretionary orders such as those made under Rule 129(1) … Moreover, in our view, when a chambers judge dismisses a motion to strike out a statement of claim, an appellate court should reverse him or her only if it is obvious without elaborate argument that there is no cause of action. 3. Alleging Negligence Equates to Alleging Fact The plaintiff alleges that the City owed a duty to her, that it breached that duty and that she suffered damages. For pleadings purposes, an allegation of negligence in a pleading is considered to be an allegation of fact: Fullowha v. Whitford (Nov. 25, 1996), C.A. 00628-C.A.00634 (N.W.T. C.A.). The court says: All of the defendants who moved argue that the amended statement of claim at key places offers something bald and without supporting detail. Some counsel allege that these are bald facts, others that they are bald conclusions. Doubtless a statement of claim must plead the necessary facts, and a mere legal conclusion is not enough. Merely to plead that the defendant is liable to the plaintiff for the tort of defamation might well not suffice, for example. That is a legal conclusion, not a fact. However, there is a big difference between pleading a mere conclusion of law and pleading a fact. To plead that the defendant negligently injured the plaintiff is to plead a fact, even if it also implies a legal conclusion… . . . . . The reasons under appeal also say that ‘Allegations which are nothing more than speculative assumptions disguised as facts are also unacceptable.’ They cite no authority for that, and we know of none. If a plaintiff pleads facts, she need not have any evidence of them. She may rely on later discovery or cross-examination at trial to yield them. A plaintiff who is knocked unconscious in a traffic accident and suffers temporary amnesia may know nothing about the accident. All of her statement of claim may be speculative assumptions. But no one would strike it out on that ground, and her speculations may well be proved accurate at the trial… . . . . . And it is customary to plead particulars of negligence, though no rule requiring that was shown to us… . . . . . Can one logically say that a statement of claim which pleads the facts which give a cause of action discloses no cause of action, because it does not give the details of when, where, or how? We reject that suggestion, and these cases agree: Paterson & Hidson v. Livingstone, [1931] 1 D.L.R. 386 (S.C.C.); Bechtel Can. v. Stearns Catalytic, [1990] A.U.D. 212, 215 (C.A.); cf. Baxter v. Calgary Sexual Assault Centre (10 Jan ‘95), Calg. # 14546 (Alta. C.A.)… The following quote, from Fullowha is a complete answer to the suggestion that insufficient facts are pled: In any event, the simple answer is that the Rules and the decided cases say that a claim should be struck out only for clear want of a cause of action, or very clear very bad abuse of process. The remedy for want of particulars is a demand for particulars, and then (if that is not answered) a motion for particulars. The court always has the power to order further particulars, but to defer giving them until after discovery. Such a power is completely inconsistent with the idea that the pleading is liable to be struck out for mere want of particulars. Peterson v. Aperocho (1996), 199 A.R. 153 (Master), at pp. 155-56, per Master Funduk. 4. Merely Alleging a Breach of a Duty at Law Is Not Enough In Tottrup v. Alberta (Minister of Environment), 2000 ABCA 121, 2000 CarswellAlta 365, 255 A.R. 204, 81 Alta. L.R. (3d) 27, Madam Justice Conrad made it clear that it is not enough for a plaintiff to allege the breach a duty. The plaintiff must plead the facts which give rise to the alleged breach (see Rule 104). At pp. 37-38, her Ladyship said: With respect, I do not agree with my colleague, Russell J.A., that the question raised in this case should wait unit a summary judgment application before examining whether a duty could be found. She concludes that the Chambers Judge erred because, in basing his decision on the grounds that the statutes did not impose any mandatory duties on the Ministers, he failed to appreciate that the pleadings also alleged a duty “at law.” She then concedes that had the pleadings alleged only a breach of duties or powers imposed by statute, then assuming no such duties existed, the claim should be struck. But, because of the bare allegation of a “duty at law,” the claim cannot be struck. This suggests that although to plead a statutory duty is insufficient to establish a cause of action (where upon examination no such duty exists) merely alleging a duty at law will suffice, even though there are no facts pled upon which a court could conclude that such a duty at law was owing. With respect, I do not agree. In my view, it is not the allegation of a duty at law that is critical, but the facts alleged supporting such a duty. For example, a statement of claim alleging only that “A” breached a duty owed to “B” thereby causing damage does not, in my view, disclose a cause of action. Pleadings are allegations of fact and, in my view, where negligence is alleged, that allegation must be supported by facts capable of sustaining a determination that a duty was owed, that an act or omission occurred breaching that duty, and that damages resulted. On a motion to strike it is the allegations of fact that must be examined to determine whether a cause of action exists. In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: 119 Only material facts, not bare allegations, need to be taken as proven under r 3.68(2)(b): Hovsepian v Westfair Foods Ltd, 2001 ABQB 700 at paras 28-29: While the Plaintiffs state that all allegations in the Claim must be taken as proved, the Defendants propose two limits on that principle: (1) bare allegations with no facts need not be taken as proved; and (2) speculative facts or those incapable of proof need not be taken as proved. In my view, the Defendants are correct on both points. Regarding the first limitation argued by the Defendants, I agree that there is no presumption that allegations not backed by facts must be taken as proved. Bare allegations are insufficient; allegations of fact are taken as proved for purposes of the striking out test. 120 In Arabi v Alberta, 2014 ABQB 295, Gill J dealt with applications to strike an action against a panoply of defendants, and he commented on the approach to take when dealing with pleadings containing numerous and complex allegations (at pars 48, 72, and 74): Arabi's action is defective on many bases, cannot succeed, and therefore must be struck. The amorphous nature of Arabi's many allegations and the large cast of Defendants means that a detailed, point-by-point analysis is not a logistically viable process. I will therefore approach Arabi's allegations by identifying a number of general legal and factual defects that, alone and in combination, mean the Arabi Civil Action cannot legally succeed or is based on an inadequate matrix of supporting facts … In evaluation of a Rule s 3.68 application the hearing judge is to presume that the alleged facts are true. This general rule has two caveats. One is that a fact is different from a bald allegation: an allegation “… that recite[s] the basic elements of the tort in very general terms but fails to provide material facts sufficient to demonstrate an intentional wrongdoing …”: GH v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24 at para 58. For example, Arabi's many allegations of a conspiracy among the Defendants are a bald allegation—he offers nothing on the context or details of that conspiracy … A second basis on which an alleged fact may be rejected is when it is simply an absurdity, or highly implausible. Arabi's complaints are also plagued by this defect of inherent improbability. For one, he alleges a broad-based conspiracy among lawyers involved in this matter, regardless of whether they are Crown Prosecutors or act on his behalf. (emphasis added) 5. When Limitation Period Not Expired Master Funduk has warned of the tactical error of applying to strike a statement of claim for disclosing no cause of action in instances when the plaintiff can sue again because the limitation period has not yet expired. In Jim Pattison Developments Ltd. v. Fudex International Inc. (1996), 45 Alta. L.R. (3d) 343 (Master), the learned Master said at p. 364: It never ceases to amaze me to see defendants applying to strike out a statement of claim on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action when the limitation period for suing has not expired. If the pleading is struck out and the limitation period has not expired the plaintiff can sue again, this time with the benefit of judicial advice on what should be pled to disclose a cause of action in law. 6. Onus The onus is on the applicant. So the burden of proof lies squarely on the shoulders of the applicant, because clearly, where there is an issue, no matter how minuscule, the plaintiff should be permitted the opportunity to have the matter tried by a trial judge. Principal Group Ltd. (Trustee of) v. Alberta (1991), 118 A.R. 40 (Q.B.), at 42, per Moore C.J.Q.B. 7. Disclosing No Defence To strike out under the first ground the statement of defence must not disclose a defence in law. One cannot, under this rule, strike out a statement of defence merely because it is felt the defendant does not have a defence in fact. The rule provides that a defence can be struck out if it discloses no defence. This is not to be confused with not disclosing a reasonable defence … The pleadings should not be struck out unless it is quite clear that no defence is disclosed… Only in the clearest possible case should a pleading be struck out. Ainge v. DeCouteau (1980), 13 Alta. L.R. (2d) 193 at 194 (Master). 8. Presumption of Truth The allegations in the pleadings must be taken as true. The allegations of the statement of claim must, of course, be taken as true for the purpose of determining the question of the disclosure of a cause of action. Western Leaseholds Ltd. v. Western Minerals Ltd. (1960), 31 W.W.R. 10 at 12 (Alta. C.A.). And Côté J.A. said: On a motion to strike out for want of a cause of action, the courts assume that the plaintiff can prove the facts pleaded… Such suits go to trial, or at least to a motion for summary judgment with evidence. Galand Estate v. Stewart (1992), 6 Alta. L.R. (3d) 399 at 408 (C.A.). In Hovsepian v. Westfair Foods Ltd., 2001 ABQB 700, 2001 CarswellAlta 1113, 296 A.R. 283, 95 Alta. L.R. (3d) 331, Mr. Justice Hart noted that there are two limits on the principle that the allegations in the Statement of Claim are to be taken as proved. At pp. 342-343, His Lordship said: While the Plaintiffs state that all allegations in the Claim must be taken as proved, the Defendants propose two limits on that principle: (1) bare allegations with no facts need not be taken as proved; and (2) speculative facts or those incapable of proof need not be taken as proved. In my view, the Defendants are correct on both points. Regarding the first limitation argued by the Defendants, I agree that there is no presumption that allegations not backed by facts must be taken as proved. Bare allegations are insufficient; allegations of fact are taken as proved for purposes of the striking out test. … Regarding the second limitation argued by the Defendants, they submit that the court is not required to assume the truth of “allegations based on assumptions or speculations”, or facts that are “patently ridiculous or incapable of proof”. These phrases come, respectively, from Operation Dismantle Inc. v. R., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441 at 455 (S.C.C.), and Air India, Re (1987), 62 O.R. (2d) 130 at 135 (Ont. H.C.). In Operation Dismantle Inc., the majority refused to consider allegations as true which were incapable of proof because they were based on assumptions or speculations as to the reactions of various governments should Canada allow the United States to test cruise missiles in Canada. The court in Air India, Re did not elaborate on its statement of “patently ridiculous”, and did not appear to need to apply that reasoning in its analysis. In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: [262] An application to strike under 3.68(2)(b) must proceed on the basis that the pleaded facts are true, unless they are manifestly incapable of proof. Those facts must also be more than bald allegations reciting the basic elements of the tort. Master Birkett quoted this statement in De Vos v. Alberta (Transportation), 2020 ABQB 234, 2020 CarswellAlta 640, 11 Alta. L.R. (7th) 97, 62 M.V.R. (7th) 237 (Master) at paragraph 47. In Broda v. Alberta, 2020 ABQB 221, 2020 CarswellAlta 623 (Master), Master Summers said: [44] Pursuant to subrule 3.68(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court no evidence may be submitted on an application under clause (b) of subrule 3.68(2). Although that subrule has been taken to mean that the statements within a plaintiff's pleading must be taken as true, there is a limit to that presumption. That is, a bare allegation, such as bad faith or malice, without any facts pled in support and without particulars, is inadequate. There is a need for descriptive evidence in support of a claim of potential wrongdoing. Nor are allegations based on assumptions or suspicions to be accepted as true: Tottrup v Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) 2000 ABCA 121; Walton International Group Inc v Rockyview (Municipal District No. 44), 2007 ABCA 21; G. H. v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24; Grenon v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2017 ABCA 96; and Clark v Hunka, 2017 ABCA 346. 9. Cross-applications to Strike and Amend Claim On appeal, counsel for the respondent conceded that where there are cross-motions to strike out a statement of claim and to amend it, the judge hearing the motions should consider the amendment motion first. And it was conceded that we should look at the proposed further amended statement of claim to see if it disclosed a cause of action. United Petroleum Distributors (Calgary) Ltd. v. 548311 Alberta (1998), 65 Alta. L.R. (3d) 346 (C.A.), at 348, per curiam. In Riccioni v. Law Society of Alberta, 2017 ABQB 261, 2017 CarswellAlta 641 (Master), Master Robertson said: 36 The law is clear that when there is an application for summary judgment and there is a cross-application to amend, the Court should consider the proposed amendment before the summary judgment application: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 208 (CanLII) at para. 27 and H. Ash & Associates v Banham, 2014 ABQB 718, [2014] A.R. 731. In my view, the same approach applies to an application to strike a claim under rule 3.68. 10. Are Consent Amendments Subject to R. 3.68 Attack? During argument, the court raised the issue of whether the plaintiff was entitled to orders pursuant to rule 129 to strike those portions of the amended statement of defence and counterclaim where the allegations had been allowed to be inserted in the pleadings by the plaintiff consenting to the order granted May 15th, 1996, by Justice C.S. Phillips. Such an order would have been granted pursuant to rule 132 which authorizes the court to allow amendments. Typically the court under rule 132 would allow an amendment through the exercise of the court's discretion to allow new facts in the matter to be introduced into the pleadings to determine the real issue between the parties. On a contested motion under rule 132, the court would exercise its discretion to allow an amendment to introduce new claims and allegations where there is a possibility that the claims and allegations would be successful. Where the court had thus considered the matter under rule 132 it is unlikely that a party having opposed an amendment under rule 132 could successfully argue that the amendment once allowed had no merit under rule 129. However, as is the case here, where the parties consent to an amendment which is approved by a court order, it is possible for counsel for the plaintiff to return to court under rule 129 to have the matter struck as having no merit. In such a case, the court in the original application for an amendment had not considered any argument that part or all of the amendments were without merit. Here, previous counsel for the Bank of Montreal had consented to the amendment and present counsel having reviewed the pleadings and discovery is entitled to apply for an order pursuant to rule 129 to have the allegations struck if there is truly no merit to the allegation. Bank of Montreal v. Peddle (1998), 214 A.R. 85 (Master), at 90, per Master Laycock.

Wilson J. considered other Supreme Court of Canada decisions and indicated that following these decisions “the test remained whether the outcome of the case was ‘plain and obvious’ or ‘beyond reasonable doubt’”.
I believe that this summary of the principles is also an enumeration of the principles used in Alberta in connection with a motion to strike under R.
129 …Rocky Mountain Rail Society v.
H & D Hobby Distributing Ltd.
L.R.
Madam Justice Fruman then drew a distinction between “novel legal propositions” (which normally are not to be struck) and “broadening a narrowly defined tort” (which might be struck).
At p.

431 of Rocky Mountain Rail Society, her Ladyship said: While judges should not be quick to strike pleadings which raise novel legal propositions, I do not see this matter as a novel proposition but rather as a broadening of a narrowly defined tort.

No public policy reasons have been suggested to justify such an extension, which would open the floodgates of this type of pleading and would put Rocky Mountain and its directors to the time and expense of defending an action that is doomed to failure.
In Manulife Financial Services Ltd. v.
BTK Holdings Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 355 (Master), Master Funduk noted that “novel” does not encompass “far-fetched”.
At p.
360, the learned Master said: It also does not help to say that a pleading should not be struck out where it raises something novel.
Novel does not encompass something that is plain and obvious beyond doubt.
The answer to that (said in another context) is: It is true that in one decision I said the test is what is arguable.
It must be understood, of course, that that means reasonably arguable.
In a sense almost any proposition (except maybe whether two plus two equals four) is arguable.
But it cannot be a far-fetched argument; it cannot be an argument that is contrary to binding authority.
(Mocyk v.
Municipal District of East Peace No.
9503-0257-A.C., Côté J.A.) Novel does not encompass far-fetched.
The Court of Appeal in Korte v.
Deloitte, Haskins & Sells (1993), 8 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 337, 1993 CarswellAlta 304, 135 A.R.
389 (C.A.), noted that specific words need not be pleaded to set forth a cause of action—the test is whether the essence of the cause of action is set forth in the pleading.
At p.

340, the court said: The court should also allow for some generosity in assessing whether the statement of claim discloses a cause of action, and it is not always necessary to plead specific words or specific legal conclusions providing that the essence of the action is outlined in the pleadings.
In Tanar Industries Ltd. v.
American Home Assurance Co.
L.R.
(3d) 144 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal noted that if a chambers judge dismisses an application under R.
129(1)(a), an appeal ought to be allowed only if it is obvious that there is no cause of action.
At p.
147, the court, per curiam, said: In addition, this Court must have regard to the standard of review that is relevant in appeals of this sort.

Appellate courts will not lightly interfere with discretionary orders such as those made under Rule 129(1) … Moreover, in our view, when a chambers judge dismisses a motion to strike out a statement of claim, an appellate court should reverse him or her only if it is obvious without elaborate argument that there is no cause of action.
Alleging Negligence Equates to Alleging Fact The plaintiff alleges that the City owed a duty to her, that it breached that duty and that she suffered damages.
For pleadings purposes, an allegation of negligence in a pleading is considered to be an allegation of fact: Fullowha v.
Whitford (Nov.
The court says: All of the defendants who moved argue that the amended statement of claim at key places offers something bald and without supporting detail.
Some counsel allege that these are bald facts, others that they are bald conclusions.
Doubtless a statement of claim must plead the necessary facts, and a mere legal conclusion is not enough.
Merely to plead that the defendant is liable to the plaintiff for the tort of defamation might well not suffice, for example.
That is a legal conclusion, not a fact.
However, there is a big difference between pleading a mere conclusion of law and pleading a fact.
To plead that the defendant negligently injured the plaintiff is to plead a fact, even if it also implies a legal conclusion… . . . . .

The reasons under appeal also say that ‘Allegations which are nothing more than speculative assumptions disguised as facts are also unacceptable.’ They cite no authority for that, and we know of none.
If a plaintiff pleads facts, she need not have any evidence of them.
She may rely on later discovery or cross-examination at trial to yield them.
A plaintiff who is knocked unconscious in a traffic accident and suffers temporary amnesia may know nothing about the accident.
All of her statement of claim may be speculative assumptions.
But no one would strike it out on that ground, and her speculations may well be proved accurate at the trial… . . . . .
And it is customary to plead particulars of negligence, though no rule requiring that was shown to us… . . . . .
Can one logically say that a statement of claim which pleads the facts which give a cause of action discloses no cause of action, because it does not give the details of when, where, or how?
We reject that suggestion, and these cases agree: Paterson & Hidson v.
Livingstone, [1931] 1 D.L.R.
386 (S.C.C.); Bechtel Can. v.
Stearns Catalytic, [1990] A.U.D.
Baxter v.
Calgary Sexual Assault Centre (10 Jan ‘95), Calg. # 14546 (Alta.

C.A.)… The following quote, from Fullowha is a complete answer to the suggestion that insufficient facts are pled: In any event, the simple answer is that the Rules and the decided cases say that a claim should be struck out only for clear want of a cause of action, or very clear very bad abuse of process.
The remedy for want of particulars is a demand for particulars, and then (if that is not answered) a motion for particulars.
The court always has the power to order further particulars, but to defer giving them until after discovery.
Such a power is completely inconsistent with the idea that the pleading is liable to be struck out for mere want of particulars.
Peterson v.
Aperocho (1996), 199 A.R.
153 (Master), at pp.
155-56, per Master Funduk.
Merely Alleging a Breach of a Duty at Law Is Not Enough In Tottrup v.
Alberta (Minister of Environment), 2000 ABCA 121, 2000 CarswellAlta 365, 255 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 27, Madam Justice Conrad made it clear that it is not enough for a plaintiff to allege the breach a duty.
The plaintiff must plead the facts which give rise to the alleged breach (see Rule 104).
At pp.

37-38, her Ladyship said: With respect, I do not agree with my colleague, Russell J.A., that the question raised in this case should wait unit a summary judgment application before examining whether a duty could be found.

She concludes that the Chambers Judge erred because, in basing his decision on the grounds that the statutes did not impose any mandatory duties on the Ministers, he failed to appreciate that the pleadings also alleged a duty “at law.” She then concedes that had the pleadings alleged only a breach of duties or powers imposed by statute, then assuming no such duties existed, the claim should be struck.
But, because of the bare allegation of a “duty at law,” the claim cannot be struck.

This suggests that although to plead a statutory duty is insufficient to establish a cause of action (where upon examination no such duty exists) merely alleging a duty at law will suffice, even though there are no facts pled upon which a court could conclude that such a duty at law was owing.
With respect, I do not agree.
In my view, it is not the allegation of a duty at law that is critical, but the facts alleged supporting such a duty.
For example, a statement of claim alleging only that “A” breached a duty owed to “B” thereby causing damage does not, in my view, disclose a cause of action.

Pleadings are allegations of fact and, in my view, where negligence is alleged, that allegation must be supported by facts capable of sustaining a determination that a duty was owed, that an act or omission occurred breaching that duty, and that damages resulted.
On a motion to strike it is the allegations of fact that must be examined to determine whether a cause of action exists.
In Al-Ghamdi v.

Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: 119 Only material facts, not bare allegations, need to be taken as proven under r 3.68(2)(b): Hovsepian v Westfair Foods Ltd, 2001 ABQB 700 at paras 28-29: While the Plaintiffs state that all allegations in the Claim must be taken as proved, the Defendants propose two limits on that principle:
(1) bare allegations with no facts need not be taken as proved; and
(2) speculative facts or those incapable of proof need not be taken as proved.
In my view, the Defendants are correct on both points.
Regarding the first limitation argued by the Defendants, I agree that there is no presumption that allegations not backed by facts must be taken as proved.
Bare allegations are insufficient; allegations of fact are taken as proved for purposes of the striking out test.

120 In Arabi v Alberta, 2014 ABQB 295, Gill J dealt with applications to strike an action against a panoply of defendants, and he commented on the approach to take when dealing with pleadings containing numerous and complex allegations (at pars 48, 72, and 74): Arabi's action is defective on many bases, cannot succeed, and therefore must be struck.
The amorphous nature of Arabi's many allegations and the large cast of Defendants means that a detailed, point-by-point analysis is not a logistically viable process.

I will therefore approach Arabi's allegations by identifying a number of general legal and factual defects that, alone and in combination, mean the Arabi Civil Action cannot legally succeed or is based on an inadequate matrix of supporting facts … In evaluation of a Rule s 3.68 application the hearing judge is to presume that the alleged facts are true.
This general rule has two caveats.

One is that a fact is different from a bald allegation: an allegation “… that recite[s] the basic elements of the tort in very general terms but fails to provide material facts sufficient to demonstrate an intentional wrongdoing …”: GH v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24 at para 58.

For example, Arabi's many allegations of a conspiracy among the Defendants are a bald allegation—he offers nothing on the context or details of that conspiracy … A second basis on which an alleged fact may be rejected is when it is simply an absurdity, or highly implausible.
Arabi's complaints are also plagued by this defect of inherent improbability.
For one, he alleges a broad-based conspiracy among lawyers involved in this matter, regardless of whether they are Crown Prosecutors or act on his behalf.
(emphasis added) 5.

When Limitation Period Not Expired Master Funduk has warned of the tactical error of applying to strike a statement of claim for disclosing no cause of action in instances when the plaintiff can sue again because the limitation period has not yet expired.
In Jim Pattison Developments Ltd. v.
Fudex International Inc.
L.R.
(3d) 343 (Master), the learned Master said at p.

364: It never ceases to amaze me to see defendants applying to strike out a statement of claim on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action when the limitation period for suing has not expired.

If the pleading is struck out and the limitation period has not expired the plaintiff can sue again, this time with the benefit of judicial advice on what should be pled to disclose a cause of action in law.
Onus The onus is on the applicant.

So the burden of proof lies squarely on the shoulders of the applicant, because clearly, where there is an issue, no matter how minuscule, the plaintiff should be permitted the opportunity to have the matter tried by a trial judge.
Principal Group Ltd.
(Trustee of) v.
Alberta (1991), 118 A.R.
40 (Q.B.), at 42, per Moore C.J.Q.B.
Disclosing No Defence To strike out under the first ground the statement of defence must not disclose a defence in law.
One cannot, under this rule, strike out a statement of defence merely because it is felt the defendant does not have a defence in fact.
The rule provides that a defence can be struck out if it discloses no defence.

This is not to be confused with not disclosing a reasonable defence … The pleadings should not be struck out unless it is quite clear that no defence is disclosed… Only in the clearest possible case should a pleading be struck out.
Ainge v.
DeCouteau (1980), 13 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 193 at 194 (Master).
Presumption of Truth The allegations in the pleadings must be taken as true.
The allegations of the statement of claim must, of course, be taken as true for the purpose of determining the question of the disclosure of a cause of action.
Western Leaseholds Ltd. v.
Western Minerals Ltd.
10 at 12 (Alta.

And Côté J.A. said: On a motion to strike out for want of a cause of action, the courts assume that the plaintiff can prove the facts pleaded… Such suits go to trial, or at least to a motion for summary judgment with evidence.
Galand Estate v.
Stewart (1992), 6 Alta.
L.R.
In Hovsepian v.
Westfair Foods Ltd., 2001 ABQB 700, 2001 CarswellAlta 1113, 296 A.R.
L.R.
Justice Hart noted that there are two limits on the principle that the allegations in the Statement of Claim are to be taken as proved.
At pp.
342-343, His Lordship said: While the Plaintiffs state that all allegations in the Claim must be taken as proved, the Defendants propose two limits on that principle:
(1) bare allegations with no facts need not be taken as proved; and
(2) speculative facts or those incapable of proof need not be taken as proved.
In my view, the Defendants are correct on both points.
Regarding the first limitation argued by the Defendants, I agree that there is no presumption that allegations not backed by facts must be taken as proved.

Bare allegations are insufficient; allegations of fact are taken as proved for purposes of the striking out test. … Regarding the second limitation argued by the Defendants, they submit that the court is not required to assume the truth of “allegations based on assumptions or speculations”, or facts that are “patently ridiculous or incapable of proof”.
These phrases come, respectively, from Operation Dismantle Inc. v.
441 at 455 (S.C.C.), and Air India, Re (1987), 62 O.R.

In Operation Dismantle Inc., the majority refused to consider allegations as true which were incapable of proof because they were based on assumptions or speculations as to the reactions of various governments should Canada allow the United States to test cruise missiles in Canada.
The court in Air India, Re did not elaborate on its statement of “patently ridiculous”, and did not appear to need to apply that reasoning in its analysis.
In Al-Ghamdi v.

Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: [262] An application to strike under 3.68(2)(b) must proceed on the basis that the pleaded facts are true, unless they are manifestly incapable of proof.
Those facts must also be more than bald allegations reciting the basic elements of the tort.
Master Birkett quoted this statement in De Vos v.
Alberta (Transportation), 2020 ABQB 234, 2020 CarswellAlta 640, 11 Alta.
L.R.
(7th) 237 (Master) at paragraph 47.
In Broda v.

Alberta, 2020 ABQB 221, 2020 CarswellAlta 623 (Master), Master Summers said: [44] Pursuant to subrule 3.68(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court no evidence may be submitted on an application under clause (b) of subrule 3.68(2).
Although that subrule has been taken to mean that the statements within a plaintiff's pleading must be taken as true, there is a limit to that presumption.
That is, a bare allegation, such as bad faith or malice, without any facts pled in support and without particulars, is inadequate.
There is a need for descriptive evidence in support of a claim of potential wrongdoing.

Nor are allegations based on assumptions or suspicions to be accepted as true: Tottrup v Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) 2000 ABCA 121; Walton International Group Inc v Rockyview (Municipal District No.
H. v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24; Grenon v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2017 ABCA 96; and Clark v Hunka, 2017 ABCA 346.

Cross-applications to Strike and Amend Claim On appeal, counsel for the respondent conceded that where there are cross-motions to strike out a statement of claim and to amend it, the judge hearing the motions should consider the amendment motion first.
And it was conceded that we should look at the proposed further amended statement of claim to see if it disclosed a cause of action.
United Petroleum Distributors (Calgary) Ltd. v.
548311 Alberta (1998), 65 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 346 (C.A.), at 348, per curiam.
In Riccioni v.

Law Society of Alberta, 2017 ABQB 261, 2017 CarswellAlta 641 (Master), Master Robertson said: 36 The law is clear that when there is an application for summary judgment and there is a cross-application to amend, the Court should consider the proposed amendment before the summary judgment application: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 208 (CanLII) at para.
27 and H.
Ash & Associates v Banham, 2014 ABQB 718, [2014] A.R.
In my view, the same approach applies to an application to strike a claim under rule 3.68.
Are Consent Amendments Subject to R.
3.68 Attack?

During argument, the court raised the issue of whether the plaintiff was entitled to orders pursuant to rule 129 to strike those portions of the amended statement of defence and counterclaim where the allegations had been allowed to be inserted in the pleadings by the plaintiff consenting to the order granted May 15th, 1996, by Justice C.S.
Phillips.
Such an order would have been granted pursuant to rule 132 which authorizes the court to allow amendments.

Typically the court under rule 132 would allow an amendment through the exercise of the court's discretion to allow new facts in the matter to be introduced into the pleadings to determine the real issue between the parties.

On a contested motion under rule 132, the court would exercise its discretion to allow an amendment to introduce new claims and allegations where there is a possibility that the claims and allegations would be successful.

Where the court had thus considered the matter under rule 132 it is unlikely that a party having opposed an amendment under rule 132 could successfully argue that the amendment once allowed had no merit under rule 129.

However, as is the case here, where the parties consent to an amendment which is approved by a court order, it is possible for counsel for the plaintiff to return to court under rule 129 to have the matter struck as having no merit.
In such a case, the court in the original application for an amendment had not considered any argument that part or all of the amendments were without merit.

Here, previous counsel for the Bank of Montreal had consented to the amendment and present counsel having reviewed the pleadings and discovery is entitled to apply for an order pursuant to rule 129 to have the allegations struck if there is truly no merit to the allegation.
Bank of Montreal v.
Peddle (1998), 214 A.R.
85 (Master), at 90, per Master Laycock.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.68(2):2 Rule 3.68(2)—“irrelevant, frivolous or improper” See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2). The new rule speaks of “irrelevant”, “frivolous”, “improper”; and an “abuse of process”. Cases dealing with the concepts of “scandalous” and “vexatious” may assist in understanding “improper” and “abuse of process”. The material must show the defence to be false beyond question before the plaintiff is entitled to have it struck out… The jurisdiction to strike out a pleading should be exercised with extreme caution and only in obvious cases. Ainge v. DeCouteau, supra, at 195. And in Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Prisco (1994), 158 A.R. 305 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice Forsyth said, at p. 320: Further, “vexatious” under rule 129(1)(b) of the Rules of Court does not encompass dealing with the merits of the defendants' claim. In Decock v. Alberta, 2000 ABCA 122, 2000 CarswellAlta 384, 255 A.R. 234, 79 Alta. L.R. (3d) 11; leave to appeal allowed (2000) 293 A.R. 388 (note) (S.C.C.) (notice of discontinuance filed September 10, 2001), Russell J.A. said, at p. 257: … it is difficult to conceive of a claim which discloses a cause of action and which could be considered scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing or an abuse of process. In Dykun v. Odishaw, 2000 ABQB 548, 2000 CarswellAlta 814, 267 A.R. 318, Lee J., at pp. 326-7, said: The Ontario High Court has determined that a proceeding is vexatious if it satisfies any of the following tests: (a) the bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding; (b) where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is vexatious; (c) vexatious actions include those brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights; (d) it is a general characteristic of vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in earlier proceedings; (e) in determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action; (f) the failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious; (g) the respondent's conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings. Lang Michener and Fabian, Re (1987), 37 D.L.R. (4th) 685 at 691 (Ont. H.C.); Winkler v. Winkler, [1991] 2 W.W.R. 369, 70 Man. R. (2d) 47 at 374 [W.W.R.] (Q.B.); affirmed [1992] 1 W.W.R. 631, 70 Man. R. (2d) 45 (C.A.). In Jamieson v. Denman (2004), 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 113 (Q.B.); additional reasons at (2004) 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 162 (Q.B.), Watson J. discussed the meaning of “vexatious” At pp 148-149, his Lordship said (footnotes omitted): I consider the word “vexatious” to carry with it a normative concept as well as a legal one. It seems to me that a party can be said to have acted in a vexatious manner, not merely that they acted in a manner which might be characterized as mean-spirited or nasty, but also that in fact the nastiness conveyed itself through to the legal process itself. In other words, that the legal process was being misused. My view of the word “vexatious” is that it connotes not simply that the party was acting without the highest of motives, or was acting in a manner which was hostile towards the other side. “Vexatious”, as a word, means to me that the litigant's mental state goes beyond simple animus against the other side, and rises to a situation where the litigant actually is attempting to abuse or misuse the legal process. This form of a normative component arises because it seems to me that proceedings which are legally possible or procedurally allowable may still be “vexatious” under my definition of the word “vexatious” for this purpose. In other words, mere bad or selfish motive might not be sufficient to establish vexatiousness. On the other hand, bad or selfish motive might likewise not be absolutely necessary to establish vexatiousness although it seems likely that bad or selfish motives would tend to co-exist with using the legal process in bad faith and vexatiously. As to the term “frivolous”, Justice Acton said at p. 160 of Haljan v. Serdahely Estate, 2008 ABQB 472, 2008 CarswellAlta 1028, 453 A.R. 337, 93 Alta. L.R. (4th) 151: 21 The Plaintiff argues that the term “frivolous” has not been defined anywhere, but connotes humour or mirth, and is “something that would make a lawyer or judge laugh.” Contrary to what the Plaintiff has alleged, the term has been defined. In Can. (M.C.I.) v. Seifert (2002), 221 F.T.R. 228 at paras. 10 and 11, the court stated: A frivolous plea is one so palpably bad that the Court needs no real argument to be convinced of that fact. Indeed, a frivolous plea is indicative of bad faith. Frivolous and vexatious pleas include those brought or carried on by a party who is not acting bona fide. Indeed it is a proceeding which will lead to no practical result. The concepts of frivolous and vexatiousness define the obviously unsustainable claim: see Attorney General of Duchy of Lancaster v. London and North Western Railway Co., [1892] 3 Ch. 274 at 277 (C.A.). The frivolous and vexatious pleading includes those which are an abuse of process: Ashmore v. British Coal Corp., [1990] 2 Q.B. 338 at 347 (C.A.). 22 The court in 876502 Ont. Inc. v. Propco Holdings (1997), 49 O.T.C. 356, ¶ 18 (Gen. Div.) indicated that: A frivolous action has been defined, however, to be one which, on its face, is so unreal that no reasonable or sensible person could bring it. A frivolous and vexatious pleading has been defined as one which is “hopeless factually”, and which it is “plain and obvious … cannot succeed”. Excelsior Life Insurance Co. v. Zurich Investments Ltd. and Drucker et al. (1988), 89 A.R. 14, 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 209, 28 C.P.C. (2d) 264 (C.A.) 23 Frivolous also has been defined in several legal dictionaries: Dictionary of Canadian Law, 3rd ed. (Scarborough: Thomson Carswell, 2004): frivolous: lacking in substance, Gouge v. Halliday (1919), 14 Alta. L.R. 296 (Alta. S.C.) frivolous and vexatious: said of a pleading which is hopeless factually and plainly cannot succeed in its purpose. Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases, 6th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwells, 2000) frivolous: futile, misconceived, hopeless or academic. Black's Law Dictionary, 8th ed. (St. Paul: Thomson West, 2004) frivolous: lacking a legal basis or legal merit; not serious, not reasonably purposeful.

10 and 11, the court stated: A frivolous plea is one so palpably bad that the Court needs no real argument to be convinced of that fact.
Indeed, a frivolous plea is indicative of bad faith.
Frivolous and vexatious pleas include those brought or carried on by a party who is not acting bona fide.
Indeed it is a proceeding which will lead to no practical result.
The concepts of frivolous and vexatiousness define the obviously unsustainable claim: see Attorney General of Duchy of Lancaster v.
London and North Western Railway Co., [1892] 3 Ch.
The frivolous and vexatious pleading includes those which are an abuse of process: Ashmore v.
British Coal Corp., [1990] 2 Q.B.
22 The court in 876502 Ont.
Inc. v.
Propco Holdings (1997), 49 O.T.C.
Div.) indicated that: A frivolous action has been defined, however, to be one which, on its face, is so unreal that no reasonable or sensible person could bring it.
A frivolous and vexatious pleading has been defined as one which is “hopeless factually”, and which it is “plain and obvious … cannot succeed”.
Excelsior Life Insurance Co. v.
Zurich Investments Ltd. and Drucker et al.
14, 59 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 264 (C.A.) 23 Frivolous also has been defined in several legal dictionaries: Dictionary of Canadian Law, 3rd ed.
(Scarborough: Thomson Carswell, 2004): frivolous: lacking in substance, Gouge v.
Halliday (1919), 14 Alta.
L.R.
296 (Alta.
S.C.) frivolous and vexatious: said of a pleading which is hopeless factually and plainly cannot succeed in its purpose.
Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases, 6th ed.
(London: Sweet & Maxwells, 2000) frivolous: futile, misconceived, hopeless or academic.
Black's Law Dictionary, 8th ed.
(St.
Paul: Thomson West, 2004) frivolous: lacking a legal basis or legal merit; not serious, not reasonably purposeful.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.68(2)(c):1 Rule 3.68(2)(c)—“irrelevant” or “improper” See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2)(c). If a pleading is relevant it is not prejudicial or embarrassing. Ainge v. De Couteau, supra, at 195. This statement was specifically approved by Wachowich A.C.J.Q.B. in Lytton v. Alberta (1999), 245 A.R. 282 at 287-88 (Q.B.). The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal said: The term “embarrassing” has been defined many times and in London (Mayor) v. Horner (1914), 3 LTR 512 at 514 … Pickford, L.J. stated as follows: I take ‘embarrassing’ to mean that the allegations are so irrelevant that to allow them to stand would involve useless expenses and would also prejudice the trial of the action by involving the parties in a dispute that is wholly apart from the issues. Meyers v. Freeholders Oil Co. (1956), 19 W.W.R. 546 at 549 (Sask. C.A.). In Alberta, Master Funduk has said: The fact that allegations by a plaintiff in her pleading may be personally embarrassing to a defendant is not of itself a ground to strike the pleading. No doubt some defendants will find the allegations against them to be personally embarrassing, particularly so if the allegations are not true. However, defendants cannot short circuit lawsuits because of their personal feelings. Embarrassing means unreasonable and prejudicial. This part of the Rule is designed to enforce intelligibility and the rules of pleadings …Holloway v. Alberta Pork Producers Development Corp. (1996), 40 Alta. L.R. (3d) 312 (Master), at 317, per Master Funduk. With respect to a counterclaim in which the claiming party seeks the same relief as is sought in another action, Power J. said in Balm v. BHC Securities Inc., 2003 ABQB 773, 2003 CarswellAlta 1301, 350 A.R. 379, at p. 384: Where a defendant files a counterclaim for relief which is the duplicate of relief being sought in a separate, earlier action, the relief should be decided in the original action and the counterclaim should be struck on the basis that the identical issue had already been raised by the defendant in the first action. Marcels Truck Service Ltd. v. Karnoth Transportation & Construction (1988) Ltd., [1993] A.J. No. 256, 142 A.R. 390 at p. 3 [A.J.] (Q.B. Master). Moore C.J.Q.B. has said: “Embarrassing” may include pleading motive, depending on the facts of the case: Schreiner v. Hamre (1980), 5 Sask. R. 76 (C.A.). Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (1997), 214 A.R. 194 (Q.B.), at 196, per Moore C.J.Q.B. Can one apply under R. 129(b) or (c) after demanding particulars? Master Breitkreuz is of the view that one cannot: … a party who serves a demand for particulars has conceded the relevance of the allegations in respect of which particulars are demanded. In my view the demand for particulars has foreclosed the issue of relevance, and it appears to be clear that regardless of how embarrassing the pleading may be in the every day use of the word “embarrassing”, it is not legally embarrassing if it is relevant. It appears that an “embarrassing” pleading in the context of R. 129, is simply a pleading of a fact, the proof of which will not be determinative in the outcome, one way or the other. Creswell v. Edmonton Journal (1986), 42 Alta. L.R. (2d) 395 at 396 (Master). Master Waller takes a different view. In Valentine v. Bee-Bell Health Bakery Ltd. (1993), 161 A.R. 1 (Master), Master Waller said at pp. 2-3: The respondent initially argues that the mere fact that the applicant has demanded particulars with respect to the impugned paragraphs, forecloses any argument that such paragraphs should be struck. He relies upon the authority of Creswell v. Edmonton Journal… With respect, I cannot agree with this view taken by my learned colleague. The purpose of the rules relating to the furnishing of further and better particulars is to limit the generality of the pleadings with a view to have the prior pleading made sufficiently distinct to enable the applicant to frame his answer thereto properly: per Boyd, C., in Smith v. Boyd (1897), 17 P.R. 463 at p. 467. Particulars once furnished [form] part of the pleadings, Millbank v. Millbank, [1990] 1 Ch. 376 at p. 385. A requirement that a plaintiff define his claim does not of necessity admit to the relevance of the claim. Indeed particulars may properly be required as a necessary step to define the claim for a striking action. The respondent must fail in this argument.
