paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.68(2)(d):1 Rule 3.68(2)(d)—Abuse of process See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.68(2)(d). 1. Not a Closed Category In J.A. Industries (Canada) Ltd. v. Highfield Development Ltd. (1998), 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 349, 1998 CarswellAlta 896, 230 A.R. 71, 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 349 (Master), Master Funduk said, at p. 360: Abuse of process is not a closed category: Hurley v. Co-operators General Insurance Co. (1998), 160 D.L.R. (4th) 645 (N.S.C.A.). There the Court says, pp. 658-59: For the purpose of this appeal, it is neither necessary, nor desirable, to define, or to limit, the phrase ‘abuse of the process of the court’, as that phrase is used in Civil Procedure Rule 14.25. It is sufficient to note, only, that the phrase, in the context of rule 14.25, contemplates that, in commencing, or maintaining, a legal proceeding, the process of the court is being misused, or is being used for an improper purpose; as opposed to an action being brought, or maintained, for the assertion of legitimate rights. In Trimove Inc. v. Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R. (6th) 5, Justice Nielsen said: 43 The Supreme Court of Canada considered the doctrine of abuse of process in its decision in Behn v Moulton Contracting Ltd, 2013 SCC 26, [2013] 2 SCR 227: 40 The doctrine of abuse of process is characterized by its flexibility. Unlike the concepts of res judicata and issue estoppel, abuse of process is unencumbered by specific requirements. In Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles (2000), 51 O.R. (3d) 481 (C.A.), Goudge J.A., who was dissenting, but whose reasons this Court subsequently approved (2002 SCC 63, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 307), stated at paras. 55-56 that the doctrine of abuse of process engages the inherent power of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a party to the litigation before it or would in some other way bring the administration of justice into disrepute. It is a flexible doctrine unencumbered by the specific requirements of concepts such as issue estoppel. See House of Spring Gardens Ltd. v. Waite, [1990] 3 W.L.R. 347 [(C.A.)], at p. 358 … One circumstance in which abuse of process has been applied is where the litigation before the court is found to be in essence an attempt to relitigate a claim which the court has already determined. See Solomon v. Smith, supra. It is on that basis that Nordheimer J. found that this third party claim ought to be terminated as an abuse of process. [Emphasis added.] In Al-Ghamdi v. Alberta, 2017 ABQB 684, 2017 CarswellAlta 2447, Justice Goss said: 123 Under r. 3.68(2)(c), a commencement document or pleading that is frivolous, irrelevant or improper may be struck. Further under r 3.68(2)(d), a commencement document or pleading that constitutes an abuse of process may also be struck. In Arabi, the Court noted that the concepts of abuse of process and frivolous and vexatious litigation are related (at para 89), citing R v Scott, [1990] 3 SCR 979 at 1007. Although r 3.68(2)(c) no longer mentions vexatious, litigation, Alberta courts have continued to strike out vexatious litigation under either r 3.68(2)(c) or (d) because “vexatious” can be said to be the same thing as impropriety and abuse of process: McMeekin v Alberta (Attorney General), 2012 ABQB 144, at para 11; Wong v. Leung, 2011 ABQB 688 at para 33. 2. Defending an Action Defending an action cannot of itself be an abuse of the process of the court. The plaintiff must make out that the defendant is using the process of the court against good faith and not bona fide. Ainge v. DeCouteau (1980) 13 Alta. L.R. 193 at 198 (Master). 3. Inherent Power of Court Aside entirely from the Rules of Court there is, I think, inherent jurisdiction vested in the court to strike out a statement of claim as being plainly an abuse of the process of the court. Poitras v. Alberta (Attorney General) (1969), 68 W.W.R. 224 at 227 Alta. T.D. 4. Court Does Not Presume Truth of Pleadings Unlike applications under R. 129(1)(a), when considering an application under R. 129(1)(d) the court will not presume that the allegations in the pleadings are true. Of course, on an application under subr. 1(a) of R. 129, to strike out a statement of claim because it discloses no cause of action, the court must take the allegations in the statement of claim as true … The court assumes that the plaintiff can prove the facts pleaded … However, we are not concerned here with an application under subr. 1(a)… We are here concerned with an application under subr. 1(d), to strike the statement of claim or dismiss the action on the ground of abuse of process… However, in relation to an application under subr. 1(d), [the learned Chambers judge] was not entitled to take the allegations in the statement of claim as true. Boudreault v. Barrett (1995), 33 Alta. L.R. (3d) 60 (C.A.), at 65, per curiam. 5. Court Can Consider All the Pleadings In Lonrho v. Fayed (No. 2), [1991] 4 All E.R. 961 (Ch. Div.) Millet, J., commented on the evidence which he was permitted to consider in respect of an application to strike out a statement of claim. He said that where the application to strike is based on the claim that it discloses no reasonable cause of action, absolutely no outside evidence may be noted. The Judge looks only to the statement of claim to determine whether it sets out a cause of action. It is quite different for an application to strike out a statement of claim on the ground that it is vexatious or an abuse of process. In this case, evidence is admissible to show that the claim is vexatious or an abuse of process. “Unless the defendant can demonstrate shortly and conclusively that the plaintiff's claim is bound to fail or is otherwise objectionable as an abuse of process of the court, it must be allowed to proceed to trial” (at 965). The Court said, “I am entitled and bound to have regard, not only to Lonrho's pleaded case and the evidence available to support it, but also to the history of the dispute.” (at 966). . . . . . … in determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action. From my consideration of these cases, I am satisfied that I am entitled to look not only at the present statement of claim but the other pleadings surrounding the plaintiff's occupation of the condominium to gain a view of the history of the dispute. Osborne v. Pinno (1997), 208 A.R. 363 (Q.B.), at pp. 366-67, per Marshall J. 6. Ulterior Motive; Collateral Advantage I turn directly to consideration of whether the pleading is an abuse of process. There is a paucity of authority from Alberta respecting abuse of process. Goldsmith v. Sperrings Ltd., [1977] 2 All E.R. 556 (C.A.) was a civil libel action brought by a businessman who was the subject of unflattering articles in a satirical magazine. He brought the action against secondary distributors of the magazine. Some of those settled, but the remaining parties brought a motion to strike the pleadings on the ground that they had not been brought bona fide for proper purposes but were an abuse of the process… Lord Justice Bridge stated: In my judgment, one can certainly go so far as to say that when a litigant sues to redress a grievance no object which he may seek to obtain can be condemned as a collateral advantage if it is reasonably related to the provision of some form of redress for that grievance. On the other hand, if it can be shown that a litigant is pursuing an ulterior purpose unrelated to the subject matter of the litigation and that, but for his ulterior purpose he would not have commenced proceedings at all, that is an abuse of process. Lord Justice Scarman stated at 582: In the instant proceedings the defendants have to show that the plaintiff has an ulterior motive, seeks a collateral advantage for himself beyond what the law offers, is reaching out ‘to effect an object not within the scope of the process’. Osborne v. Pinno (1997), 208 A.R. 363 (Q.B.), at p. 366, per Marshall J. 7. Where Second Action Constitutes Abuse of Process A second action which is continuing while the first still exists is an abuse of process. … it [is] plainly an abuse to allow a second action to continue while the other is in good standing… The test in these matters was set out… under the following two conditions: 1. Continuance of the action would work an injustice because it would be oppressive or vexatious or an abuse of process in some other way, and; 2. The stay must not cause an injustice to the plaintiff. The burden of proof of both these conditions is on the person asking for the stay. The word oppressive has been legally defined as usually referring to deliberate acts of moral, although not necessarily legal, delinquency such as an unfair abuse of power by the stronger party in order that a weaker party may be put in difficulties in obtaining his just rights. Vexatious was said to involve overtones of an irresponsible pursuit of litigation by someone who either knows he has no proper cause of action or is mentally incapable of forming a rational opinion on the topic. It has been suggested that a liberal interpretation of what is vexatious and oppressive ought to be adopted and the court has stated that either attitude amounted to an abuse of process. See Mohler v. Dairy Queen of Western Canada Ltd. et al., [1976] 3 W.W.R. 620, an Alberta Appellate Division case … Abuse of process clearly applies where there is a multiplicity of proceedings, such as two or more law suits for virtually the same matter. Whitehead v. Taber (1983), 46 A.R. 14 at 16 (Q.B.). And in Edmonton Northlands v. Edmonton Oilers Hockey Corp. (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 179 (Q.B.), Moore C.J.Q.B. said at pp. 185-86: The courts of Alberta generally recognize a rule against multiple prosecution. It is trite law that commencing a second action while one is currently pending is an abuse of process: German v. Major (1985), 39 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (C.A.). Since the same relief can be obtained in the first action, Northlands is not entitled to bring a second action while the first is still pending: Great Pacific Contracting Ltd. v. Harwyn Properties (1981), 29 B.C.L.R. 145 (S.C.). In my view, the second action must be set aside. If the first action has been dismissed for want of prosecution, then a second action is not an abuse of process. This argument evades the fundamental issue, which is whether a second lawsuit is an abuse of process if a prior lawsuit for the same cause of action is effectively dismissed for want of prosecution. The present answer to that, in Alberta, is no. Birkett v. James, [1978] A.C. 297 (H.L.), and Department of Transport v. Chris Smaller (Transport) Ltd., [1989] 2 W.L.R. 578 (H.L.), say that if a first lawsuit is dismissed for want of prosecution the plaintiff can sue again. The dismissal of the first lawsuit for want of prosecution is not a bar to a second lawsuit. Res judicata does not apply. Birkett and Department of Transport were accepted in Alberta Government Telephones v. Arrow Excavators & Trenchers (1972) Ltd. (1989), 69 Alta. L.R. (2d) 332 (C.A.) (“A.G.T.”). In that case there was inordinate delay, the delay was inexcusable and the defendant was likely to be seriously prejudiced by the delay. Without more, the lawsuit should have been dismissed. It was not because the court said that the plaintiff could just sue again. The result would have been different if the plaintiff could not have sued again. Birkett addresses the issue whether it is an abuse of process to start a second lawsuit if the first lawsuit is dismissed for want of prosecution. It says that it is not. Department of Transport refused to depart from Birkett in any way and the second case has been followed by A.G.T. Sinclair Timber Industries Ltd. v. Métis Assn. Regional Council—Zone No. 1 (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 279 (Master), at 281-82, per Master Funduk. With respect to a counterclaim in which the claiming party seeks the same relief as is sought in another action, Power J. said in Balm v. BHC Securities Inc., 2003 ABQB 773, 2003 CarswellAlta 1301, 350 A.R. 379, at p. 384: Where a defendant files a counterclaim for relief which is the duplicate of relief being sought in a separate, earlier action, the relief should be decided in the original action and the counterclaim should be struck on the basis that the identical issue had already been raised by the defendant in the first action. Marcels Truck Service Ltd. v. Karnoth Transportation & Construction (1988) Ltd., [1993] A.J. No. 256, 142 A.R. 390 at p. 3 [A.J.] (Q.B. Master). 8. Res Judicata Principal seeks to strike the statement of claim on the basis that all issues raised in this matter had been previously finally determined by a court of competent jurisdiction. The principle of res judicata applies to bar repetitive continuing litigation on the same cause of action. It applies to issues of law and fact which were the subject matter of express judicial determination in an action between the same parties. It applies also to matters which were not specifically dealt with, but which must implicitedly [sic] have been decided because the decision could not have been made without a determination of that issue. Finally, all matters which should have been raised but which were not raised in defence of the action (with certain exceptions) are barred once a final decision is granted. Malik v. Principal Savings & Trust Co. (1985), 63 A.R. 109 (Q.B.), at 113, per McFadyen J. And Kerans J.A. said: Res judicata can extend to matters that ought to have been raised; it is not restricted to issues actually determined on the merits. Terroco Industries Ltd. v. Viking Oilfield Supply Ltd. (1987), 57 Alta. L.R. (2d) 62 at 64 (C.A.). Côté J.A. has said: It suffices to dispose of this suit to say that any and all of the matters now raised, reasonably could have been raised at the latest, in the 1984 suit by the village against the same parties. (If any could not, then that would only be because they should have been raised in the first suit.) Res judicata is not limited to what was argued and decided in the previous suit. It extends to what reasonably should have been raised. Litigation by instalments is interminable. Argentia Beach (Summer Village) v. Warshawski (1991), 84 Alta. L.R (2d) 202 at 203 (C.A.). In 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 269 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal considered the topic of res judicata. At pp. 276-77, Mr. Justice O'Leary, speaking for the court, said: Estoppel by res judicata is a rule of evidence. Where a final judicial decision has been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter “… any party or privy to such litigation, as against any other party or privy thereto, and in the case of a decision in rem, any person whatsoever, as against any other person, is estopped in any subsequent litigation from disputing or questioning such decision on the merits”: Spencer Bower and Turner, The Doctrine of Res Judicata (2nd ed.), at p. 9. The two forms of estoppel by res judicata are described in Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada, at p. 997. The first is commonly called “issue estoppel” and is defined as follows: … any action or issue which has been litigated and upon which a decision has been rendered cannot be refuted in a subsequent suit between the same parties or their privies. This principle prevents the contradiction of that which was determined in the previous litigation, by prohibiting the relitigation of issues already actually addressed. [Emphasis in original] The second is “cause of action estoppel”: The second principle makes it mandatory that a plaintiff asserting a cause of action must claim all possible relief in respect thereto and prevents any second attempt to invoke the aid of the courts in the same cause. It is sometimes called ‘merger’ because the plaintiff's cause of action becomes ‘merged’ in the judgment. The judgment actually operates as a comprehensive declaration of the rights of all parties in respect of the matters in issue. As a result, the rule applies equally to a defendant who must put forward all defences which will defeat the plaintiff's action, and the defendant who does not will be debarred from raising them subsequently. This principle prevents the fragmentation of litigation by prohibiting the litigation of matters that were never actually addressed in the previous litigation, but which properly belonged to it. [Emphasis in original] A prior judicial decision will not raise an estoppel by res judicata, either issue estoppel or cause of action estoppel, unless (i) it was a final decision pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter; (ii) the decision was, or involved, a determination of the same issue or cause of action as that sought to be controverted or advanced in the present litigation; and (iii) the parties to the prior judicial proceeding or their privies are the same persons as the parties to the present action or their privies. The court in 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal, at pp. 286-87, then made the following comments about abuse of process: The Court of Queen's Bench has power under R. 129 and its inherent jurisdiction to strike out an action as an abuse of process. The power is discretionary and its exercise will not be interfered with on appeal unless it was unreasonable. An attempt to re-litigate issues already decided or deemed to have been decided may be found an abuse of process and barred in circumstances where estoppel by res judicata is not available, for example where only one of the parties to the later action was a party to the earlier one … In Solomon v. Smith (1987), [1988] 1 W.W.R. 410 … the Manitoba Court of Appeal struck out an action on the ground that it was an abuse of process in circumstances where estoppel by res judicata was not applicable. In language apt to the case at Bar, Lyon J.A., said at p. 421: I agree … that a plea of issue estoppel is not available. However to permit the statement of claim to proceed would be an abuse of process and that is the principle applicable. In considering this doctrine, it seems to me prudent to avoid hard and fast, institutionalized rules such as those which attach to the plea of issue estoppel. By encouraging the determination of each case on its own facts against the general principle of the plea of abuse, serious prejudice to either party as well as the proper administration of justice can best be avoided … we must be vigilant to ensure that the system does not become unnecessarily clogged with repetitious litigation of the kind here attempted. There should be an end to this litigation. To allow the plaintiff to retry the issue of misrepresentation would be a classic example of abuse of process—a waste of time and resources of litigants and the court and an erosion of the principle of finality so crucial to the proper administration of justice. In Wavel Ventures Corp. v. Constantini (1996), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 292, the Court of Appeal again had before it the issue of res judicata. Having referred with approval to O'Leary J.A.'s decision in 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 269 (C.A.), McFadyen J.A. said at pp. 306-307: The rule of res judicata is not absolute in application. In some limited circumstances, a party may be permitted to enter upon new proceedings which contest a decision of an earlier court, even if the tests stated above are met. One such exception occurs when fraud is practised upon the court… In Canada, the test to be met by a party seeking to establish that exception to res judicata was stated by Garrow J. in Jacobs v. Beaver (1908), 17 O.L.R. 496 at 506 (C.A.). The fraud relied on must be something collateral or extraneous, and not merely the fraud which is imputed from alleged false statements made at the trial, which were met by counter-statements by the other side, and the whole adjudicated upon by the court and so passed on into the limbo of estoppel by the judgment. This estoppel cannot be disturbed except upon the allegation and proof of new and material facts, and from which are to be deduced the proposition that the former judgment was obtained by fraud. ..... A second exception to the res judicata principle may apply on the discovery of new evidence. That exception, however, is very limited in scope. It is not the simple acquisition of fresh evidence which permits a party to escape the consequences of the principle of res judicata. Ritchie J. in Grandview (Town) v. Doering, [1976] S.C.R. 621 at p. 636 adopted the following passage from the decision of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in Fenerty v. Halifax (City) (1920), 53 NS.R. 457 C.A., at 463: The doctrine of res judicata is founded on public policy so that there may be an end of litigation, and also to prevent the hardship to the individual of being twice vexed by the same cause. The rule which I deduce from the authorities is that a judgment between the same parties is final and conclusive not only as to the matters dealt with, but also as to questions which the parties had the opportunity of raising. It is clear that the plaintiff must go forward in the first suit with his evidence; he will not be permitted in the event of a failure to proceed with a second suit on the ground that he has additional evidence. In order to be at liberty to proceed with a second suit he must be prepared to say: I will show you this is a fact which entirely changes the aspect of the case, and I will show you further that it was not, and could not by reasonable diligence have been ascertained by me before. (Emphasis added) In Escobar v. Yacey (1998), 229 A.R. 278 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Johnstone discussed res judicata as it applies to settlements between the parties. At p. 284, Her Ladyship said: The House of Lords in Jenkin v. Robertson, [1867] L.R. 1 Sc. & Div. 117 (H.L.) … held that a compromise, agreement or such arrangement of the parties, without judicial examination of its merits, cannot form the basis of res judicata. This decision was followed in Hair v. Meaford (Town) (1914), 31 O.L.R. 124 (C.A.) and illustrates the distinction between a court acting in an administrative capacity or acting in a more explicitly judicial capacity. Lord Romilly in Jenkin… referred to the meaning of res judicata as a judicial pronouncement. Lord Romilly stated the requirement …“the court has exercised its judicial mind, and has come to the conclusion that the one side or the other side is right, and has pronounced a decision accordingly.” If the court simply “registers” the agreement of the parties, res judicata cannot be invoked on the basis of that agreement. . . . . . An order of the court can be distinguished from a contract between or among parties which may be deemed a “settlement agreement”. Master Funduk, in Angeltvedt v. Lawes et al. (1994), 164 A.R. 201 (Q.B. Master), stated that settlement agreements are not “judgments”. In that case, the determination of the status of the settlement was relevant in determining the responsibilities of the third party once the issue between the plaintiff and the defendant had been settled. A settlement agreement of that kind is in a different category than those that are taken to the court to be affixed with the court's imprimatur. If such occurs, the agreement of the parties has been transformed into a decision of the court. The status of consent agreements as final judgments has been noted in the cases of Bank of Montreal v. Coopers Lybrand Inc. and Ostapowich (1996), 144 Sask. R. 207 (C.A.) and Wensel v. Wensel et al. (1975), 65 D.L.R. (3d) 327 (Alta. T.D.). In the first case, the court definitively states that a consent judgment is a “final decision of the court.” A consent agreement is not simply approved by the court as a formality, but is addressed independently by the court, before it receives its status as a judgment. In 688560 Alberta Ltd. v. Genesis Land Developers Ltd., 2000 CarswellAlta 203, 82 Alta. L.R. (3d) 236, Verville J., at pp. 241-242, said: The doctrine of res judicata is defined succinctly in Schacher v. National Bailiff Services (January 20, 1999), Doc. Edmonton 9603-18327, 9703-11746 (Alta. Q.B.), at para. 27: The Common (sic) law doctrine of estoppel by res judicata is a rule of evidence. Where a final decision has been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties to, and the subject of, the litigation, any party or privy to such litigation, as against any other party or privy thereto is estopped in any subsequent litigation from disputing or questioning such decision on the merits, whether it be used as the foundation of an action, or relied upon as a bar to any claim, indictment or complaint, or to any affirmative defence, case, or allegation. … … Lee J. in Schacher, … states: The true test then of the doctrine of res judicata is identity of issue. The question is whether or not the judgment is conclusive, not merely as to the point actually decided but as to any matter which it was necessary to decide and which was actually decided as the groundwork of the decision itself, though not directly the point at issue. The Court is entitled to look at the pleadings, the reasons for judgment and the formal judgment to determine with precision, the issues decided. 9. Collateral attack and abuse of process In Trimove Inc. v. Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R. (6th) 5, Trimove sued Servus Credit Union alleging that Servus breached the loan agreements it had with Trimove when Servus appointed a receiver and liquidated assets of Trimove. Servus applied for an order striking out the Statement of Claim on the grounds that it did not disclose a cause of action, it constituted a collateral attack on the receivership order, and was an abuse of process. Justice Nielsen struck part of the Statement of Claim, and gave this summary of the law relating to applications to strike pleadings in such circumstances: 68 I note that most of the above cases involved applications for summary judgment. Nevertheless, a number of the general principles flowing from them are relevant to this application to strike pleadings: 1. the principle of collateral attack generally makes an order of a court having jurisdiction binding and conclusive, and not susceptible to attack in a proceeding where the object of that proceeding is other than the reversal, variation or nullification of the order or judgment: Behn, Nash 2. if an order is obtained by fraud, non-disclosure or misleading disclosure, it can be challenged directly by an application to set it aside or by appeal, but not collaterally: Got, McDonald 3. a lender may be liable where it improperly obtained a receivership order, for example, where: (a) the lender seeks both a preservation and realization order on the same day as it issues its demand for repayment, with no explanation as to why little notice was given, nor any indication of a cause for urgency or inability of the debtor to pay the debt: Got (b) the lender misleads the Court in relation to its communications with the debtor in relation to enforcing its security, and the risk to recovery: Got 4. a borrower may raise an allegation that the lender reneged on a forbearance agreement in response to an application for the appointment of a receiver: Tassone 5. a challenge to the propriety of an ex parte receivership order may be brought by way of a counterclaim in the receivership action: Got, McDonald 6. a post-receivership action against a lender is a collateral attack on orders granted in the receivership proceedings if those orders were not appealed: Got, McDonald 7. a post-receivership defence to a claim for deficiency by the lender is not barred by issue estoppel or estoppel by conduct if the defence is based on the bank's conduct prior to the proceedings to appoint a receiver: Ross 8. in considering the failure to challenge decisions in a receivership, a court may take into account that the speedy sale of assets may be in everyone's interests in order to minimize the potential loss due to an allegedly improper interim receiver order, and that a trial would significantly slow down the fulfillment of the receiver's mandate set in motion by that interim order: Ross 9. where the debtor does not appeal the receivership order, subsequent claims that the lender's actions led to the loan default and that the receiver improperly disposed of the project are belated collateral attacks (absent proven fraud) if the essence of the proposed claims would directly conflict with aspects of the receivership and sale orders: Cheema 10. failure to appeal or to apply to set aside or vary a receivership order will not bar a viable claim against the lender where attempts were made to appeal the receivership orders within the proper time period, and counsel agreed the debtor could raise the allegations contained in the statement of defence and counterclaim in the receivership action as a defence in the trial of a subsequent action by the lender for outstanding indebtedness: Got, Nahal 11. a post-receivership suit against a lender is hopeless and cannot possibly benefit an insolvent debtor unless it can yield a cash recovery exceeding the debtor's debt to the lender, as any recovery up to that sum would merely reduce the insolvent debtor's debts: Cheema 12. it is an error to strike post-receivership pleadings as an abuse of process if the pleadings, evidence and parties' agreements in the record are unclear as to relevant circumstances in the receivership proceedings: Ross.

658-59: For the purpose of this appeal, it is neither necessary, nor desirable, to define, or to limit, the phrase ‘abuse of the process of the court’, as that phrase is used in Civil Procedure Rule 14.25.

It is sufficient to note, only, that the phrase, in the context of rule 14.25, contemplates that, in commencing, or maintaining, a legal proceeding, the process of the court is being misused, or is being used for an improper purpose; as opposed to an action being brought, or maintained, for the assertion of legitimate rights.

Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R.

Unlike the concepts of res judicata and issue estoppel, abuse of process is unencumbered by specific requirements.

(3d) 481 (C.A.), Goudge J.A., who was dissenting, but whose reasons this Court subsequently approved (2002 SCC 63, [2002] 3 S.C.R.
307), stated at paras.

55-56 that the doctrine of abuse of process engages the inherent power of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a party to the litigation before it or would in some other way bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
It is a flexible doctrine unencumbered by the specific requirements of concepts such as issue estoppel.
See House of Spring Gardens Ltd. v.
Waite, [1990] 3 W.L.R.

358 … One circumstance in which abuse of process has been applied is where the litigation before the court is found to be in essence an attempt to relitigate a claim which the court has already determined.
See Solomon v.

193 at 198 (Master).

556 (C.A.) was a civil libel action brought by a businessman who was the subject of unflattering articles in a satirical magazine.

366, per Marshall J.

Q.B.), at para.
27: The Common (sic) law doctrine of estoppel by res judicata is a rule of evidence.

Where a final decision has been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction over the parties to, and the subject of, the litigation, any party or privy to such litigation, as against any other party or privy thereto is estopped in any subsequent litigation from disputing or questioning such decision on the merits, whether it be used as the foundation of an action, or relied upon as a bar to any claim, indictment or complaint, or to any affirmative defence, case, or allegation. … … Lee J. in Schacher, … states: The true test then of the doctrine of res judicata is identity of issue.

The question is whether or not the judgment is conclusive, not merely as to the point actually decided but as to any matter which it was necessary to decide and which was actually decided as the groundwork of the decision itself, though not directly the point at issue.
The Court is entitled to look at the pleadings, the reasons for judgment and the formal judgment to determine with precision, the issues decided.
Collateral attack and abuse of process In Trimove Inc. v.
Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50, 2017 CarswellAlta 88, 44 C.B.R.
(6th) 5, Trimove sued Servus Credit Union alleging that Servus breached the loan agreements it had with Trimove when Servus appointed a receiver and liquidated assets of Trimove.

Servus applied for an order striking out the Statement of Claim on the grounds that it did not disclose a cause of action, it constituted a collateral attack on the receivership order, and was an abuse of process.

Justice Nielsen struck part of the Statement of Claim, and gave this summary of the law relating to applications to strike pleadings in such circumstances: 68 I note that most of the above cases involved applications for summary judgment.

Nevertheless, a number of the general principles flowing from them are relevant to this application to strike pleadings: 1. the principle of collateral attack generally makes an order of a court having jurisdiction binding and conclusive, and not susceptible to attack in a proceeding where the object of that proceeding is other than the reversal, variation or nullification of the order or judgment: Behn, Nash 2. if an order is obtained by fraud, non-disclosure or misleading disclosure, it can be challenged directly by an application to set it aside or by appeal, but not collaterally: Got, McDonald 3. a lender may be liable where it improperly obtained a receivership order, for example, where:

(a) the lender seeks both a preservation and realization order on the same day as it issues its demand for repayment, with no explanation as to why little notice was given, nor any indication of a cause for urgency or inability of the debtor to pay the debt: Got

(b) the lender misleads the Court in relation to its communications with the debtor in relation to enforcing its security, and the risk to recovery: Got 4. a borrower may raise an allegation that the lender reneged on a forbearance agreement in response to an application for the appointment of a receiver: Tassone 5. a challenge to the propriety of an ex parte receivership order may be brought by way of a counterclaim in the receivership action: Got, McDonald 6. a post-receivership action against a lender is a collateral attack on orders granted in the receivership proceedings if those orders were not appealed: Got, McDonald 7. a post-receivership defence to a claim for deficiency by the lender is not barred by issue estoppel or estoppel by conduct if the defence is based on the bank's conduct prior to the proceedings to appoint a receiver: Ross 8. in considering the failure to challenge decisions in a receivership, a court may take into account that the speedy sale of assets may be in everyone's interests in order to minimize the potential loss due to an allegedly improper interim receiver order, and that a trial would significantly slow down the fulfillment of the receiver's mandate set in motion by that interim order: Ross 9. where the debtor does not appeal the receivership order, subsequent claims that the lender's actions led to the loan default and that the receiver improperly disposed of the project are belated collateral attacks (absent proven fraud) if the essence of the proposed claims would directly conflict with aspects of the receivership and sale orders: Cheema 10. failure to appeal or to apply to set aside or vary a receivership order will not bar a viable claim against the lender where attempts were made to appeal the receivership orders within the proper time period, and counsel agreed the debtor could raise the allegations contained in the statement of defence and counterclaim in the receivership action as a defence in the trial of a subsequent action by the lender for outstanding indebtedness: Got, Nahal 11. a post-receivership suit against a lender is hopeless and cannot possibly benefit an insolvent debtor unless it can yield a cash recovery exceeding the debtor's debt to the lender, as any recovery up to that sum would merely reduce the insolvent debtor's debts: Cheema 12. it is an error to strike post-receivership pleadings as an abuse of process if the pleadings, evidence and parties' agreements in the record are unclear as to relevant circumstances in the receivership proceedings: Ross.

sentences.text: Joining claims

paragraphs.text: (1) A party may join 2 or more claims in an action unless the Court otherwise orders. (2) A party may sue or be sued in different capacities in the same action. (3) If there is more than one defendant or respondent, it is not necessary for each to have an interest (a) in all the remedies claimed or sought, or (b) in each claim included in the action.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.69:1 Rule 3.69 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.69. 1. Permissive Nature of Rule Rule 32 allows a plaintiff to unite several causes of action in one action. However it does not require him to do so. Bank of Nova Scotia v. Guenette (1986), 75 A.R. 361 at 368 (Master). One action may contain alternative claims based on different causes of action. See Elliott v. Barry (1920), 15 Alta. L.R. 329 (C.A.). Also, Hyndman J.A. said: I had thought that there was no doubt about the right to rely upon and claim several different rights “alternatively although they may be inconsistent”… … the plaintiff may claim alternative remedies and is not put to his election until his right to relief is established either after default of defence when he may prove for judgment, or after the evidence is concluded on a trial. Campbell v. Munro (1922), 17 Alta. L.R. 272 at 275, 276 (C.A.). Where a plaintiff was suing in contract on six separate invoices, including interest charges, Master Funduk stated: I have already concluded that each is a separate contract. The plaintiff is uniting six causes of action in this action, which is permissible: R. 32. Satelite Painting Enterprises Ltd. v. Yukon Trailer Service Ltd. (1992), 85 Alta. L.R. (2d) 328 at 331 (Master).

paragraphs.text: 3.70. Parties joining to bring action
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Parties joining to bring action

paragraphs.text: (1) Two or more parties may join to bring an action, and a plaintiff or originating applicant may make a claim against 2 or more persons as defendants or respondents in an action, if (a) the claim arises out of the same transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences, (b) a question of law or fact common to the parties is likely to arise, or (c) the Court permits. (2) This rule applies irrespective of the remedy claimed by the plaintiff or originating applicant and whether or not 2 or more plaintiffs or originating applicants seek the same remedy.
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: (1) Two or more parties may join to bring an action, and a plaintiff or originating applicant may make a claim against 2 or more persons as defendants or respondents in an action, if

(b) a question of law or fact common to the parties is likely to arise, or

paragraphs.text: 3.71. Separating claims
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Separating claims

paragraphs.text: (1) When 2 or more claims are made in an action or when 2 or more parties join or are joined in an action, the Court may make an order under this rule if the Court is satisfied that the joined claims or parties, or both, may (a) unduly complicate or delay the action, or (b) cause undue prejudice to a party. (2) The Court may, by order, do one or more of the following: (a) order separate trials, hearings, applications or other proceedings; (b) order one or more of the claims to be asserted in another action; (c) order a party to be compensated by a costs award for having to attend part of a trial, hearing, application or proceeding in which the party has no interest; (d) excuse a party from having to attend all or part of a trial, hearing, application or proceeding in which the party has no interest.

sentences.text: (1) When 2 or more claims are made in an action or when 2 or more parties join or are joined in an action, the Court may make an order under this rule if the Court is satisfied that the joined claims or parties, or both, may
